title: The Product Management Mistake That Happens Before the First User Story

The CEO has an idea, the sales team asks for a feature, or the support team suggests a fix for recurring complaints. The next steps seem obvious: clarify the request, write user stories, define acceptance criteria, and work with design and engineering to deliver the solution. The backlog is updated. The requirements are clear. The team knows what to build. But one question may still be unanswered: Are we solving the right problem in the first place? Understanding the Problem Behind a Request One common mistake in product management is treating a requested solution as if it were a clear definition of the problem. Imagine a sales manager saying: “Our customers need higher credit limits. We should increase the credit available to them.” That request contains a hypothesis: insufficient credit is preventing customers from purchasing. Before accepting it, we need to investigate. Which customers are reaching their limits? Are they abandoning purchases because they cannot access more credit? Or are they struggling with a complicated purchasing journey, missing suppliers, or a product that offers too little value? Different customers may face different constraints. If credit limits are the real obstacle for a particular group, increasing them might help. If those customers are not using their existing credit, we need to understand why before offering more. The request is a useful starting point. It gives us something to investigate, but it does not establish which solution will create value. The Hidden Cost of Solving the Wrong Problem A feature can work exactly as designed, meet every acceptance criterion, and launch on schedule, yet fail to produce the expected business outcome. The consequences can include: · Wasted engineering capacity: Time spent on an ineffective solution is time unavailable for more valuable work. · Unnecessary complexity: Additional features can make a product harder to use and maintain. · Stakeholder misalignment: Teams can agree on what to build while holding different assumptions about why it is needed. · Loss of trust: When promised outcomes repeatedly fail to materialize, stakeholders may question the team’s decisions. In these cases, excellent execution cannot compensate for a poorly understood problem. What to Clarify Before Committing to Development Before committing substantial development time, I believe product teams should use the following four checks. These guide a shared investigation rather than a rigid sequence. Drafting a user story can help expose uncertainty, and discovery should continue as the team learns. 1 Define the Problem Clearly Start by asking, “What is happening, and why does it matter?” A useful problem statement should clarify: · Who is experiencing the problem? · In what context does it occur? · What is happening today? · What outcome are we trying to improve? “Users need better reporting” gives us little to work with. A more useful problem statement might be: “Sales managers cannot identify inactive customers early enough to follow up promptly, reducing opportunities to re-engage them.” This identifies a user, an obstacle, and a consequence to investigate. It leaves room for several possible solutions, including changes that do not require a new dashboard. 2 Separate Assumptions From Evidence Product managers rarely have perfect information. We still need to distinguish what we know from what we believe. Depending on the question, useful evidence might come from customer interviews, product analytics, funnel analysis, support tickets, or operational data. Competitor research can suggest alternatives, but it does not establish what our own users need. For the credit-limit request, we could examine utilization and abandoned purchases among the customers reporting the problem, then speak with some of them about what prevented a purchase. We should also ask what evidence would make us reconsider the proposed solution. That helps keep the investigation open to findings that challenge our initial assumptions. The aim is to reduce the uncertainty that matters most to the decision. 3 Define Success Before Committing to an Output Launching a sales dashboard is an output. Reducing the time needed to identify inactive customers is an outcome. Increasing the proportion of those customers who purchase again is a further outcome the dashboard might support. Before investing in the solution, clarify: · The primary success metric and its current baseline · The target improvement and evaluation timeframe · The assumptions connecting the solution to the outcome · The unwanted effects we need to monitor For example, a credit-limit change should be evaluated alongside repayment performance, not purchase growth alone.
